abstract.p: Precision psychiatry aims to identify biomarkers and develop prediction models to improve diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. Despite extensive research, translating findings into clinically useful tools remains challenging. Here we argue that one important contributor to this translational gap is a pervasive misalignment between routine statistical analytic practices and the requirements for real-world decision making. To help address this, we introduce predictive utility analysis: a statistical workflow for estimating the practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by accounting for outcome base rates and measurement reliability. Starting from effect size or model performance estimates, the workflow simulates expected real-world performance in a target population and summarizes it across complementary metrics including positive and negative predictive value, Precision-Recall AUC, and Net Benefit. Analogous to how power analysis is used for determining the conditions needed to achieve statistical significance, predictive utility analysis can help determine the conditions needed to achieve practical significance. We implement and illustrate this workflow using E2P Simulator, a recently developed open-source web tool that makes predictive utility analysis accessible through interactive simulations and publication-ready visualizations. We demonstrate its application using specific examples in three key areas: diagnostic (depression, Alzheimer’s disease), treatment response (antidepressants), and risk (suicide attempts and psychosis onset) prediction, highlighting conditions under which we may expect clinically meaningful advances. While we focus on translational challenges in psychiatry, the workflow and tools presented here address general statistical challenges and are broadly applicable across biomedical and behavioral sciences.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The search for clinically useful psychiatric biomarkers has been a major pursuit of the past several decades, spanning structural and functional neuroimaging, genetic and multiomic approaches, cognitive and computational assays, and, more recently, digital and deep phenotyping (Singh and Rose, 2009; García-Gutiérrez et al., 2020; Jollans and Whelan, 2018; Abi-Dargham et al., 2023; Stephan and Mathys, 2014; Onnela and Rauch, 2016; Clark et al., 2025). With the emergence of precision medicine (Council et al., 2011; Collins and Varmus, 2015), these efforts have recently culminated in the vision of precision psychiatry: the idea that accounting for individual variability across different modalities can help go beyond broad diagnostic categories and trial-and-error treatments, towards more personalized mental health care (Fernandes et al., 2017; Bzdok and Meyer-Lindenberg, 2018; Rutledge et al., 2019; Patzelt et al., 2018; Huys et al., 2016; Paulus and Thompson, 2021; Karvelis et al., 2023; Van Dellen, 2024).

Despite extensive research and methodological advances, real-world clinical impact of individualized prediction models remains difficult to achieve (Salazar de Pablo et al., 2021). While there is a lot of excitement in the field, with many empirical studies reporting high predictive accuracy, a more critical look suggests that this optimism may be misplaced: overfitting (Meehan et al., 2022; Chekroud et al., 2024; Tornero-Costa et al., 2023; Bracher-Smith et al., 2021), small sample sizes, and biased validation methods are the rule rather than the exception (e.g., Karvelis et al., 2022; Schnack and Kahn, 2016; Hunt et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025). When it comes to individual biomarkers, most of them have also failed to replicate or prove their clinical utility (Abi-Dargham et al., 2023; Cortese et al., 2023).

A natural question arises: what is holding back progress? While many factors are at play (Kambeitz-Ilankovic et al., 2022; Felsky et al., 2023), here we argue that one crucial bottleneck is a pervasive misalignment between routine statistical analysis practices and the requirements for clinical translation. Most common analytic approaches are optimized for identifying the existence of effects (p-values, model evidence), while effect sizes, which convey practical significance, often receive much less attention (Loth et al., 2021; Kapur et al., 2012; Wasserstein et al., 2019; Lo et al., 2015; Flora, 2020). Even when effect sizes are reported and discussed (e.g., in meta-analyses), their meaningful interpretation often poses a problem (Funder and Ozer, 2019). The situation is further exacerbated by how effect sizes and thus their translational value are attenuated by measurement reliability, which often goes unassessed and unaddressed (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025a; Karvelis et al., 2023; Hedge et al., 2018). When multiple predictors of small effect sizes are then combined to build prediction models, they end up underperforming (which is often masked by inflated performance metrics due to overfitting). On top of that, predictive performance is often evaluated using metrics (e.g., sensitivity, specificity) (Cortese et al., 2023) that do not account for real-world outcome base rates (e.g., prevalence, response rates) and therefore do not convey their real-world predictive value (Abi-Dargham and Horga, 2016; Carter et al., 2017; Jeni et al., 2013; Brabec et al., 2020; Foody, 2023; Guesné et al., 2024) or clinical utility (Rousson and Zumbrunn, 2011). Although these problems are documented in the literature and many are addressed by guidelines such as TRIPOD (Moons et al., 2015; Collins et al., 2024) and STARD (Bossuyt et al., 2015), a lack of accessible tools for dealing with them presents ongoing challenges for the wider research community.

In what follows, we first examine how these methodological challenges limit the interpretation and clinical translation of biomarkers and prediction models in precision psychiatry (Fig. 1). We then introduce predictive utility analysis, a statistical workflow for evaluating practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by accounting for real-world outcome base rates and measurement reliability. We illustrate its application using E2P (effect-to-prediction) Simulator, www.e2p-simulator.com (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025b), a recently developed open-source web tool that enables to perform this analysis via interactive simulations. To demonstrate its use, we present worked examples from three key areas: diagnostic, treatment response, and risk prediction, highlighting important insights along the way.

caption.title: Precision psychiatry: from individual differences to clinical prediction.
caption.p: The path to precision psychiatry begins with research on individual differences, which exist across many dimensions. The first challenge is to develop tools to measure and characterize these differences (phenotyping). Next, clinically relevant differences must be identified (biomarker research). Finally, collections of relevant markers can be used to build prediction models. However, systemic problems in research practices (highlighted in red) at multiple steps in this pathway undermine progress.

sec.title: Statistical challenges in understanding practical significance
2.1 Statistical significance is not practical significance
sec.p: Research in psychiatry and behavioral sciences is dominated by null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST) and p-values, which have well-known limitations (Kirk, 1996; Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017; Ioannidis, 2005; Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016; Wasserstein et al., 2019; Yarkoni, 2022; Meehl, 1992; Kapur et al., 2012). Most problematically, based solely on statistical significance, researchers often conclude that their findings have potential for clinical utility - but significant variables are not automatically good predictors (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016; Lo et al., 2015; Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017; Kapur et al., 2012; Loth et al., 2021; Kühberger et al., 2015). The same limitations apply to more sophisticated measures of Bayesian model evidence (Stephan et al., 2009; Friston et al., 2016; Palminteri et al., 2017; Wilson and Collins, 2019) - both approaches simply quantify the confidence in the existence of the effects, but not their strength (Fig. 2). In the age of increasingly large datasets, this is problematic because increasingly smaller and thus more practically negligible effects become the focus of scientific inquiry (Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017; Marek et al., 2022). To be able to gauge the translational value of research findings, it is therefore important to focus on the estimation and interpretation of effect sizes (Calin-Jageman, 2018; Flora, 2020; Nakagawa and Cuthill, 2007).

caption.title: Different levels of research questions with associated methods and metrics.
caption.p: Much of the research planning and clinical translation strategy is currently formulated based on the mere existence of effects. This can be misleading, as translational potential is proportional not to statistical significance or model evidence, but to effect size. These observed effects can be further expressed as discriminative ability and - by accounting for real-world base rates - as predictive value and clinical utility. Each subsequent step becomes increasingly informative for gauging translational potential, as conveyed by the emojis.

sec.title: 2.2 Poor measurement reliability attenuates effect sizes and predictive utility
sec.p: The lack of focus on effect size interpretation also leads to overlooking the importance of measurement reliability, which attenuates observed effects. This is particularly problematic in psychiatry, where many constructs - from cognitive (Karvelis et al., 2023; Enkavi et al., 2019), to neuroimaging (Elliott et al., 2020; Nikolaidis et al., 2022; Gell et al., 2024; Vidal-Piñeiro et al., 2025), to diagnostic categories themselves (Regier et al., 2013) - are measured with substantial unreliability.

For correlational analysis, the attenuation of observed effects by poor measurement reliability has been long established (Spearman, 1904):
robserved=rtrueICCx⋅ICCy,
(1)

where ICCx and ICCy denote the reliabilities of the two variables expressed as Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). However, this attenuation is rarely accounted for in routine analyses in psychiatry. The attenuation effects are considered even less in the context of group differences (e.g., patients vs. controls), where the formulae describing them were not established until very recently (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025a); for a general case considered in this paper:
dobserved=dtrue2ICC1⋅ICC2ICCl+ICC2sin(π2κ),
(2)

where the observed Cohen’s d is attenuated by both predictor reliability in each of the groups (ICC1 and ICC2) and the reliability of the group labels themselves (measured as Cohen’s κ; e.g., inter-rater agreement).

Given that poor measurement reliability makes the groups overlap more, we would expect it to have important consequences in predictive modeling. Yet, its effects have been explored only by a small number of studies (Gell et al., 2024; Nikolaidis et al., 2022; Jacobucci and Grimm, 2020; Whittle et al., 2018; Lionetti et al., 2025; Cullen et al., 2023). As we will see later, the nature of the E2P Simulator allows anyone to explore these effects without needing to code their own simulation pipelines.

sec.title: 2.3 The challenge of interpreting effect sizes
sec.p: Even when effect sizes are reported, researchers struggle to interpret them in a meaningful way. The most common approach is to simply rely on conventional levels of small (d = .2, r = .1), medium (.5, .3), and large (.8, .5) - however, these labels are arbitrary, do not convey translational potential, and were never meant to be used so ubiquitously (Funder and Ozer, 2019; Anvari et al., 2023; Carey et al., 2023; Correll et al., 2020; Giner-Sorolla et al., 2024; Rothman and Greenland, 2018; Durlak, 2009). Another common approach is to compare observed effects with other empirical findings in one’s research domain (Lovakov and Agadullina, 2021; Thompson, 2007; Durlak, 2009; Gignac and Szodorai, 2016; Bosco et al., 2015). Although this may serve as a more meaningful reference point, empirically reported effect sizes are often inflated due to publication bias (Schäfer and Schwarz, 2019), and, even more importantly, they do not directly convey practical significance (Giner-Sorolla et al., 2024; Kirk, 1996; Kapur et al., 2012). Given that our ultimate goal is to build prediction models to personalize psychiatry, practical significance is best understood in terms of predictive performance (Shmueli, 2010).

sec.title: 2.3.1 ROC-AUC, sensitivity, specificity
sec.p: Expressing effect sizes in terms of prediction metrics is actually quite straightforward. All we need is to draw a classification threshold between the two groups and determine true and false positives and negatives - all prediction metrics are then derived from these four categories (see Fig. 3). The most common metrics are sensitivity (true positive rate, or proportion of cases correctly identified) and specificity (true negative rate, or proportion of non-cases correctly identified). Moving the threshold across the whole range captures how these metrics trade off against one another, which is captured by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Calculating the area under ROC (ROC-AUC) provides an informative summary metric which captures the average probability that, given a randomly chosen positive and a randomly chosen negative individual (e.g., a patient with a psychiatric condition and a control), a predictor assigns a higher predicted risk score to the positive than to the negative.

caption.p: Standardized mean difference measures, such as Cohen’s d, capture how far the two distributions are from each other. If we place a decision threshold (red) to classify cases into two groups, there are four possible outcomes: True Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), False Negatives (FN), and True Negatives (TN). These four outcomes are used to derive all classification metrics, as presented on the right. In predictive utility analysis, we place a special emphasis on PR-AUC and NB (highlighted in blue), as they can convey both overall and context-specific model performance while accounting for real-world base rate, making them highly informative for understanding the translational potential of research findings.

Even more straightforwardly, ROC-AUC can be computed directly from Cohen’s d:

sec.title: 2.4 Prediction metrics can be misleading if real-world outcome base rate is not accounted for
sec.p:
While ROC-AUC, sensitivity, and specificity are useful metrics for assessing a predictor’s discriminative performance, they may create a misleading impression of translational potential because these metrics are invariant to outcome base rates (e.g., disease prevalence, treatment response rate, event rate). This is problematic because in clinical contexts many decisions occur under low or varying prevalence (Carter et al., 2017; Abi-Dargham and Horga, 2016). When prevalence is low, most predicted positives will be false - this phenomenon and the associated mistakes are known as the false positive paradox, base rate fallacy, and base rate neglect (Casscells et al., 1978; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973; Tversky and Kahneman, 1974). The relevant metric in such cases is the posterior probability of disease given a positive test, which is most commonly known as positive predictive value (PPV):
PPV=ϕ⋅Sensitivityϕ⋅Sensitivity +(1−ϕ)⋅(1−Specificity),
(4)
where ϕ is the base rate.

When base rates are low, achieving high PPV (also known as precision) is only possible at the expense of sensitivity (also known as recall). This trade-off is more transparently summarized by the area under the Precision-Recall curve (PR-AUC), which has been argued to be a more informative metric for imbalanced classification contexts (Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015; Cartus et al., 2023; Ozenne et al., 2015; Pinker, 2018), although see Van Calster et al. (2025).

However, PR-AUC itself can be misleading when models are evaluated on artificially balanced groups, which is common practice (Jeni et al., 2013; Brabec et al., 2020; Foody, 2023; Guesné et al., 2024). In such cases, the reported PR-AUC reflects the base rate of the test set rather than the deployment conditions. If the full ROC curve or sensitivity and specificity across thresholds are available, precision can be recalculated at each threshold using the expected real-world base rate in Eq. 4, yielding an estimated PR-AUC for deployment conditions (Brabec et al., 2020).

sec.title: 2.4.1 Real-world outcome base rates in Decision Curve Analysis
sec.p:
The challenge of accounting for real-world outcome base rates extends beyond standard prediction metrics to more clinically oriented evaluation frameworks, such as decision curve analysis (DCA) (Vickers and Elkin, 2006). DCA is based on calculating Net Benefit (NB), a clinical utility metric which balances true positives (TP) by weighing them against the potential harms of false positives (FP; e.g., overdiagnosis or overtreatment):
NB=TPN−FPN⋅pt1−pt
(5)

where pt represents the probability threshold used for classification (representing the relative cost of false positives compared to the benefit of true positives) and N is the total number of cases. It can also be expressed in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and base rate ϕ:
NB=Sensitivity⋅ϕ−(1−Specificity)⋅(1−ϕ)⋅pt1−pt.
(6)

In DCA, NB is plotted against a range of probability thresholds, creating a decision curve that shows the net benefit of using the model compared to two alternative strategies: “all” (classifying everyone as positive) and “none” (classifying everyone as negative). The difference in NB between model-based predictions and the default “all” and “none” lines (ΔNB) conveys how much additional clinical utility the model can offer at relevant thresholds. An optimal threshold would reflect the costs of false negatives versus the costs of false positives. For example, a very low threshold (e.g., <5%) is appropriate for suicide risk screening in primary care where the intervention (e.g., safety planning) is low-cost but missing a case is fatal (Ross et al., 2021), whereas a high threshold (e.g., >50%) is required for initiating clozapine in early psychosis due to monitoring costs and side effects (Farooq et al., 2024).

DCA is an increasingly popular method for evaluating clinical prediction models, has desirable decision-theoretic properties (Van Calster et al., 2025), and is recommended by the TRIPOD guidelines (Moons et al., 2015; Collins et al., 2024). However, just as with PR-AUC, NB can be severely inflated if models are evaluated on artificially balanced case-control samples (Rousson and Zumbrunn, 2011). Fortunately, these estimates can also be adjusted post-hoc to reflect real-world base rates without requiring model retraining.

sec.title: 2.5 Predictive utility analysis and E2P Simulator
sec.p: To bring these statistical considerations together, we introduce predictive utility analysis: a statistical workflow for evaluating the practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by explicitly accounting for real-world outcome base rates,measurement reliability, and, where relevant, the decision threshold. The workflow can be thought of as consisting of two key components: (1) translating conventional effect size and model performance metrics into measures that more directly reflect expected predictive value and utility, including PPV, NPV, PR-AUC, and NB by accounting for real-world base rates and relevant clinical decision thresholds, and (2) determining how much performance is lost due to measurement reliability.

Predictive utility analysis can be used both to evaluate existing findings and to inform research planning (Box 1). When evaluating an existing finding, researchers can work forward from a reported effect size or model performance estimate to examine its expected predictive value and utility in the target population. When planning research, they can work backward from a desired level of predictive performance (Lord et al., 2019) to determine which combinations of effect size or discriminative performance, measurement reliability, outcome base rate, and number of predictors would achieve that target. This is analogous to power analysis (Cohen, 1992): whereas power analysis evaluates whether a study is likely to detect an effect under specified assumptions, predictive utility analysis evaluates whether an effect or model is likely to provide meaningful practical utility under specified assumptions.

caption.title: Predictive utility analysis: evaluating findings and planning research

tr.td:
A. Evaluating existing findings Begin with an observed finding and work forward to estimate its predictive value and utility in the intended target population.
Specify measurement reliability. Enter reliability estimates for the predictor and outcome, preferably from the same dataset or closely matched studies. A value of 1 assumes perfect reliability and therefore excludes attenuation due to measurement error from the analysis.
Enter the observed result. Use an effect size (e.g., Cohen’s d, OR, Pearson’s r) or predictive-performance metric (e.g., ROC-AUC, PR-AUC). Prefer a robust or conservative estimate that is unlikely to be inflated by a small sample or overfitting.
Specify the target population. Use the outcome base rate expected where the predictor or model will be applied, rather than the proportion of cases in the study sample. The target population and, for risk prediction, the time horizon should align with those used to estimate the observed effect.
Define the decision threshold. Specify the predicted probability at which a result would prompt clinical action. The threshold should be lower when missing a case is more consequential and higher when unnecessary action carries greater harm or burden. Under a simplified cost formulation, pt = CFP/(CFP + CFN), where CFP and CFN represent the costs of false positives and false negatives, respectively.
Summarize predictive utility. Report ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, PPV, NPV, and Net Benefit at the chosen threshold, together with the corresponding visualizations. Also report the estimated loss of performance attributable to measurement unreliability.

B. Planning future research Begin with a clinically meaningful performance target and work backward to determine the predictor properties and application context needed to achieve it.
Define the performance target. Specify clinically meaningful values of PR-AUC, PPV, NPV, or Net Benefit, informed by cost-benefit analysis, clinical guidelines, or the performance of existing instruments. Select a decision threshold appropriate to the consequences of false positives and false negatives.
Specify the intended setting. Define the expected outcome base rate and measurement reliability in the population where the predictor or model would be used.
Estimate the required effect size or discrimination performance. Adjust the effect size or model discrimination until the performance target is reached, then compare the required value (e.g., Cohen’s d or ROC-AUC) with realistic estimates from the literature or pilot data.
Evaluate possible improvements. Test whether the target could be reached through more reliable measurements, multiple predictors, or application in a clinically appropriate higher risk population. Any higher base rate scenario should remain consistent with the population in which the underlying effects are estimated. For multivariable models, use plausible effect sizes and collinearity estimates (see Supplementary note 2).
Report feasible scenarios. Present the combinations of effect size, reliability, base rate, decision threshold, and number of predictors that achieve the target, and assess the practical feasibility of each combination.

sec.p: To make this workflow accessible and intuitive, we recently developed an interactive open-source web tool, E2P Simulator (www.e2p-simulator.com) (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025b). E2P Simulator provides an interactive interface for converting among effect-size metrics (e.g., Cohen’s d, Pearson’s r), discrimination metrics (e.g., ROC-AUC, sensitivity, specificity), predictive-value metrics (e.g., PRAUC, PPV, NPV), decision-analytic metrics (e.g., Net Benefit), and other related quantities while accounting for measurement reliability and outcome base rates. All metrics are derived from the same visualized data distributions, making their relationships more intuitive (see Supplementary note 1 for the calculations and assumptions). E2P Simulator also provides publication-ready figures, supports transparent reporting, and serves educational purposes.

sec.title: Demonstration of predictive utility analysis with E2P Simulator
sec.p: The examples in this section demonstrate how predictive utility analysis and E2P Simulator can be applied across a variety of translational contexts, and the kinds of insights that it can provide.

sec.title: 3.1.1 A cognitive marker for depression
sec.p: Consider finding a cognitive biomarker with Cohen’s d = 0.8 between healthy controls and a group diagnosed with depression. Such an effect size is rare in practice and would be interpreted as “large”; e.g., some of the strongest biomarkers, such as negative interpretation bias and decreased autobio graphical memory specificity, are d < 0.8 (Weiss-Cowie et al., 2023; Everaert et al., 2017). But how would that translate to diagnostic prediction?

First, we have to account for the inter-rater reliability of the depression diagnosis, which is κ = 0.28 as determined by DSM-5 field trials (Regier et al., 2013). For the biomarker itself, we will assume ICC = 0.6 test-retest reliability, in line with the average reliability of cognitive markers in recent studies (Karvelis et al., 2023). Finally, because the effect size in question summarizes the differences between patients and healthy controls, the relevant target population for this illustrative analysis is the general population. Recent national surveys estimate depression prevalence to be around 9.2% among Americans aged 12 years or older (Goodwin et al., 2022) and 7.7% among Canadians aged 15 years or older (Halladay et al., 2026). We therefore use 8% as a rounded illustrative base rate within this range. Note that a more clinically realistic scenario, such as those explored below, would consider the biomarker in a preselected, higher prevalence group (e.g., help-seeking individuals); however, evaluating the biomarker in this setting would require an effect size estimated using controls drawn from that same target population rather than healthy controls from the general population.

With these parameters, the observed Cohen’s d = 0.8 will yield ROC-AUC = 0.71 and PR-AUC = 0.19 (Fig. 4a). While conventionally 0.8 would be called “large”, the predictive utility is modest as indicated by the low PR-AUC, which captures the trade-off between PPV and sensitivity. We next consider a screening application in which individuals with a predicted probability of depression above pt = 0.15 are referred for further diagnostic assessment. This threshold assumes that unnecessary referral has a relatively low cost compared with failing to identify a person with depression. This results in PPV = 0.22 and sensitivity = 0.31, meaning that at this threshold, 78% of predicted cases would be false positives, and 69% of actual cases would still be missed. This would correspond to ANB = 0.009 or 9 additional true positives per 1,000 people evaluated.

caption.p: (a) A cognitive marker for depression, (b) the FDA-cleared Lumipulse G p-tau217/Aβ42 plasma test for amyloid pathology. Both figures are screenshots of E2P Simulator’s interface showing inputs on the left (effect size metrics, reliability values, and the base rate), the resulting data distributions in the center, and all predictive and utility metrics at the bottom and on the right. sec.p: We can then explore the consequences of a hypothetical improvement in measurement reliability. If both the biomarker and diagnostic outcome were measured perfectly, the expected effect would increase to d = 1.58, with substantially better predictive performance: ROC-AUC = 0.87, PR-AUC = 0.46, PPV = 0.34, sensitivity = 0.63, and ΔNB = 0.033 at pt = 0.15. This illustrates how much diagnostic prediction could improve through better measurement alone.

sec.title: 3.1.2 Combining multiple biomarkers to improve diagnostic prediction
sec.p: E2P Simulator also includes multivariable calculators that estimate how many biomarkers of a given strength and collinearity would be required to achieve a specified performance target, assuming an additive linear model without interaction effects (see Supplementary note 2 for more details). Let us use an illustrative target of PR-AUC = 0.80, which at 8% prevalence corresponds to ROC-AUC = 0.96. Using the multivariable simulator, we find that with small collinearity among the predictors (0.05), this would require 20 predictors, without collinearity (0.00), it would still require 10 d = 0.8 predictors, while with stronger predictors of d = 1.35, even with a higher collinearity of 0.1, we would need only 5 to achieve the same target performance (Supplementary Fig. 1). This suggests that focusing on identifying larger effects (e.g., by improving measurement reliability) may be a more promising research strategy than searching for additional predictors that are weak (think multi-modal big data approaches).

sec.title: 3.1.3 FDA-cleared p-tau217/Aβ42 plasma test for Alzheimer’s disease
sec.p: To provide a reference point for the previous example, let us consider an example from precision medicine: the Lumipulse G p-tau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio, the first blood test cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to aid identification of amyloid pathology associated with Alzheimer’s disease (FDA, 2025b). It is indicated for adults aged ≥ 50 years with cognitive symptoms in specialized care (FDA, 2025a). The test uses separate classification thresholds for positive and negative results, with values between them classified as indeterminate. In the 499-person study, this approach yielded PPV = 91.8% and NPV = 97.3% against amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), with 19.6% of results classified as indeterminate.

Let us recreate this biomarker in E2P Simulator to obtain a clear picture across all metrics. The prevalence of amyloid positivity in the study was 51.1% (FDA, 2025a). Test-retest reliability of the device was not reported, but repeated measurements of related p-tau217 and Aβ42 assays show high reliability (ICC = 0.76–0.97) (Della Monica et al., 2024); we therefore use ICC1 = ICC2 = 0.9 as a rough approximation for the ratio . Inter-rater reliability of amyloid PET also tends to be high (κ > 0.9) (Harn et al., 2017); because the reference standard was either PET or CSF, we use κ ≈ 0.9 as a rough approximation. We then jointly set the effect size and decision threshold to reproduce PPV w 92% and NPV ≈ 81% at the positive cutoff, treating indeterminate results as non-positive (201 true positives, 18 false positives, 54 false negatives, and 226 true negatives).

We find that this performance corresponds to an observed Cohen’s d = 2.25, ROC-AUC = 0.94, and PR-AUC = 0.95 (similar results were also reported in a recent study in China by Wang et al. (2025), achieving ROC-AUC ≈ 0.96); the classification threshold in this case corresponds to pt = 0.68, which gives ΔNB = 0.327 (Fig. 4b). In real-world settings, we may expect the prevalence to be lower or at least to vary: for cohorts with mild cognitive impairment, amyloid positivity ranges from ~30% at the age of 50 to ~ 60% at the age of 80 (Jansen et al., 2015). However, even at 30% prevalence, d = 2.25 would still result in an impressive PR-AUC = 0.89.

sec.title: 3.2.1 Multivariable neurocognitive predictors of antidepressant response
sec.p: Can we predict treatment response to antidepressants? Research using multivariable / machine learning models suggests that neurocognitive predictors (brain activity and behavioral measures derived from cognitive tasks) can explain 20% of the variance (R2 = 0.2) in symptom improvement in response to antidepressants and other treatments (Karvelis et al., 2022). While this already combines multiple predictors and may be an optimistic estimate due to overfitting issues, let us consider what this would translate to in practice.

For this illustration, we use ICCx =0.4 as a rough proxy for the reliability of the composite prediction score, based on the average reliability of task-evoked fMRI measures (Elliott et al., 2020), and ICCy = 0.95 as an optimistic proxy for symptom-change reliability, based on the reported inter-rater reliability of MADRS total scores (Geijer et al., 2021). A recent meta-analysis of SSRI trials reported a 46% response rate, defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in MADRS scores (Hieronymus et al., 2025); we therefore use 46% as the base rate.

Entering these values into E2P Simulator yields ROC-AUC = 0.71 and PR-AUC = 0.66, indicating rather modest predictive performance, as shown by the low PR-AUC (Fig. 5). We use an illustrative threshold of pt = 0.20 to examine classification of likely responders among patients receiving antidepressant treatment. At pt = 0.2, we observe sensitivity = 0.98 and PPV = 0.48, meaning that 88% of nonresponders would still be classified as likely responders. This would correspond to ΔNB = 0.005 or 5 additional correctly identified responders per 1,000 patients evaluated. Under these proxy reliability assumptions, perfect measurement would improve performance quite substantially, up to ROC-AUC = 0.85 and PR-AUC = 0.83, which at pt =0.2 would result in sensitivity = 0.95, PPV = 0.59, and ΔNB = 0.035.

sec.p: Using E2P Simulator we find that to achieve PR-AUC = 0.8, it would require explaining approximately 47% of variance (R2 = 0.47), which is rather ambitious. This nicely demonstrates the well-known problems of dichotomizing continuous measures (Collins et al., 2016; MacCallum et al., 2002; Royston et al., 2006; Naggara et al., 2011; Streiner, 2002; Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025a). When symptom improvement on a continuous scale gets converted to responders vs. non-responders, a lot of the information gets lost. This is important to highlight, because most research on treatment response prediction continues to use dichotomized outcome measures (Karvelis et al., 2022; Vieira et al., 2022; Amleshi et al., 2025).

sec.title: 3.2.2 Combining multiple biomarkers to improve treatment response prediction
sec.p: When building prediction models in neuroscience, a common approach is to first show that candidate biomarkers are associated with clinical variables (e.g., symptom severity), after which both are jointly used to train a classifier for predicting clinical outcomes (e.g., Hauke et al., 2022; Tozzi et al., 2020; de la Salle et al., 2022; Karvelis et al., 2022). Because these predictors may capture overlapping information, collinearity can limit the incremental predictive gain obtained by combining them. For example, assuming an average collinearity of 0.15 among all predictors, we would need 20 predictors of r = 0.3 to achieve PR-AUC = 0.8, which translates to R2 = 0.47 (Supplementary Fig. 2). Interestingly, if we reduce the effect size of each predictor to r = 0.25, we would never reach R2 = 0.47, no matter how many predictors we have (Supplementary Fig. 2).

sec.title: 3.3.1 Mismatch negativity (MMN) as a predictor of psychosis conversion in at-risk individuals
sec.p: Most research on predictive modeling in psychiatry has thus far focused on predicting the transition to psychosis (Salazar de Pablo et al., 2021), with positive and negative symptoms and verbal memory deficits being the most prominent clinical and cognitive predictors, and mismatch negativity (MMN) emerging as the most promising biomarker (Andreou et al., 2023; Rosen et al., 2021).

How promising is MMN for predicting the transition to psychosis? The primary intended clinical application of MMN is as a prognostic tool within already identified clinical high-risk (CHR) groups. The largest longitudinal study measured MMN at baseline and, after 24 months of follow-up, found that, among participants not taking antipsychotic medication at baseline, converters showed the largest deficit in the double-deviant (duration + pitch) condition, with an effect size of d = 0.43 (Hamilton et al., 2022). Over a 24-month follow-up period, the average transition rate in CHR cohorts is about 19% (De Pablo et al., 2021). Within-site reliability for double-deviant MMN is approximately G = 0.5, which we use as a rough proxy for ICC = 0.5 (Roach et al., 2020). We use κ = 0.46 as a rough proxy for outcome reliability, based on the test-retest reliability of DSM-5 schizophrenia diagnosis (Regier et al., 2013).

Putting this all together with E2P Simulator, we find that double-deviant MMN provides only modest predictive performance within CHR cohorts: ROC-AUC = 0.62 and PR-AUC = 0.27 (Fig. 6a). At an illustrative decision threshold of pt = 0.15, corresponding to relatively low-cost interventions such as increased monitoring, the net benefit is ΔNB = 0.011, with PPV = 0.22 and sensitivity = 0.81. Improving measurement reliability could improve performance up to ROC-AUC = 0.70, PR-AUC = 0.36; at pt = 0.15 this would give PPV = 0.27, sensitivity = 0.77, ΔNB = 0.028. These numbers highlight that MMN offers incremental discrimination but remains far from sufficient as a stand-alone biomarker.

Both figures are screenshots of E2P Simulator’s interface showing inputs on the left (effect size metrics, reliability values, and the base rate), the resulting data distributions in the center, and all predictive and utility metrics at the bottom and on the right. sec.p: These estimates also need to be considered within the broader context. CHR criteria - based on subthreshold psychotic symptoms, brief episodes, family risk, functional decline - identify only about 6–7% of people who will later develop psychosis (Talukder et al., 2025), meaning that CHR criteria already miss more than 93% of people who will later develop psychosis, substantially limiting the added value of MMN in identifying psychosis risk, and suggesting that a more pressing challenge may be to develop more sensitive CHR criteria.

sec.title: 3.3.2 Predicting 12-month suicide risk using baseline electronic health records
sec.p: Clinicians rate prediction of suicidality as the highest priority for AI tool development in mental health (Fischer et al., 2025). While many predictive models have been developed using cross-sectional suicidality data (Pigoni et al., 2024), only a few have used baseline predictors to estimate prospective risk. Edgcomb et al. (Edgcomb et al., 2021) developed models using a cohort of 1,628 women with serious mental illness and 8,408 index general hospitalizations for primary non-psychiatric medical diagnoses (12-month event rate: 1.3%), then evaluated them externally in a cohort of 140,848 women and 841,834 such hospitalizations (event rate: 4.8%). The models predicted readmission for suicide attempt or intentional self-harm from pre-discharge electronic health records, achieving ROC-AUCs of 0.73 in the derivation sample and 0.71 in the external sample. A companion study in men (N = 1.4 million) reported similar results (AUC ≈ 0.73 in the derivation sample) (Thiruvalluru et al., 2023).

Because external validation better reflects how the model performs in a new clinical setting, we focus on the external cohort and pair its ROC-AUC of 0.71 with its corresponding event rate of 4.8%. We assume near-perfect reliability for the recorded readmission outcome (κ ≈ 1). The prediction score was derived from structured electronic health record variables, including healthcare utilization, prior suicide attempts, and psychiatric diagnoses. We assume that these routinely recorded variables are relatively reliable and, on this basis, use ICC1 = ICC2 = 0.8 as an illustrative value for the reliability of the resulting multivariable score in women with and without the outcome.

Using these inputs, ROC-AUC = 0.71 yields PR-AUC = 0.12 (Fig. 6b). At an intervention threshold of pt = 3%, sensitivity is 0.85, specificity is 0.40, PPV is 0.07, and ΔNB is 0.004. Thus, this operating point would identify 85% of qualifying readmissions, but only 7% of flagged hospitalizations would be followed by such a readmission; the incremental net benefit over intervening for everyone is small. Achieving PR-AUC = 0.80 in this population would require ROC-AUC = 0.98. At pt = 0.03, this would yield sensitivity = 0.94, PPV = 0.30, and ΔNB = 0.023.

We should also consider the fact that many studies compare attempters to healthy controls, not psychiatric controls. In such cases, a predictor or predictive model should be evaluated using the prevalence of suicide attempts in the general population, where the 12-month prevalence is 0.3%— around 16 times lower than the 4.8% event rate in the external hospital cohort (Borges et al., 2010). Such low prevalence, however, makes prediction in the general population extremely difficult.

The challenges that low prevalence poses for predicting suicide attempts are well-known Carter et al. (2017); Kessler et al. (2020), so our results here are not surprising. However, we hope that it will help clarify the fundamental prediction challenges for those who continue to work on suicide risk prediction. Considering that the ultimate goal is to reduce suicide rates, improving universal prevention methods may be more productive than developing tools for individual risk assessment (Quinlivan et al., 2017; Steeg et al., 2018).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this paper, we highlighted a number of statistical pitfalls that are undermining clinical translation efforts and introduced predictive utility analysis together with E2P Simulator to help researchers navigate these challenges. We provided detailed examples of how predictive utility analysis can help interpret existing findings and plan future research in three key areas: diagnostic, treatment response, and risk prediction. We showed that even seemingly large effect sizes (Cohen’s d) or strong discrimination performance (ROC-AUC) can yield modest predictive value and clinical utility when accounting for real-world outcome base rates. We also showed that poor measurement reliability can be a significant factor in attenuating predictive performance - a research area that remains understudied (Gell et al., 2024; Jacobucci and Grimm, 2020; Whittle et al., 2018; Cullen et al., 2023; Schulz and Ritter, 2026). Overall, these observations point to the need to improve measurement reliability and to identify larger effects in order to move closer towards translational goals. This echoes recent calls to find ways to increase effect sizes in neuroimaging and psychiatry research to improve statistical power (DeYoung et al., 2025; Makowski et al., 2024; Jahanshad et al., 2025), but here we directly connect this need to translational challenges.

Although we focused on precision psychiatry to convey our points, the ideas and tools we introduce are relevant for many areas in health research concerned with diagnostic test development, biomarker research, screening instruments, and prediction models (Van Calster et al., 2025; Collins et al., 2025; Leeflang et al., 2013; Maxim et al., 2014; Monsarrat and Vergnes, 2018; McGeechan et al., 2008; Hicks et al., 2022; Rutledge and Loh, 2004), and could also be meaningfully applied in many other areas, including forensic psychology (Weber et al., 2025), law (Kirk, 2019; Chin, 2023), and education (Glutting et al., 1997). All these research areas grapple with the challenge of interpreting effect sizes, and using them to inform policy and real-world decision making.

sec.title: 4.1 Selecting appropriate inputs for predictive utility analysis
sec.p: Predictive utility analysis is informative only to the extent that its inputs are carefully and appropriately chosen. Effect sizes from individual studies are subject to sampling error and may be inflated by publication bias, selective reporting, or analytical flexibility (Button et al., 2013; Ioannidis, 2008; Ioannidis and Panagiotou, 2011). Similarly, estimates of multivariable model performance may be overly optimistic because of overfitting (e.g., Karvelis et al., 2022; Schnack and Kahn, 2016; Hunt et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025) or confounding features (Chyzhyk et al., 2022; Komeyer et al., 2025). This creates a tricky paradox: while our analysis shows that larger effect sizes are needed for clinical translation, many effects reported in the literature may already be inflated. To guard against these issues, researchers should use the most robust estimates available: effect sizes should ideally be supported by large samples, replication, or meta-analysis, while model performance should be estimated using properly held out or external validation data.

Selecting an appropriate measurement reliability estimate also requires care. First, measurement reliability remains underreported and underassessed (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025a; Karvelis et al., 2023; Hedge et al., 2018; Parsons et al., 2019), so a relevant estimate may not always be available. Second, the reliability of a given instrument can vary across versions, populations, and administration contexts (e.g., Cooper et al., 2017), meaning that an available estimate may not generalize to the intended application. Third, reliability can be estimated in different ways, and not all estimates are equally informative for a given use case. For example, interrater reliability of DSM diagnoses computed from clinicians rating the same recorded interviews can be higher than estimates based on repeated independent interviews (Chmielewski et al., 2015); however, the latter is more relevant because it better reflects the reliability of repeated assessments in real-world contexts (Regier et al., 2013), and that is what we used in our examples. Finally, reliability estimates can themselves be uncertain when based on small samples (Williams et al., 2025).

Disease prevalence estimates can also vary substantially with study design, geographic region, cohort composition, and estimation method (e.g., Simeone et al., 2015; Flor et al., 2020). When base rates are very low, obtaining precise estimates becomes especially difficult (McGrath and Burke, 2024). For predictive utility analysis to be informative, two considerations are essential. First, the selected base rate must correspond to the population represented by the effect size or model performance estimate, because these quantities are not independent (Leeflang et al., 2013, 2009; Moons et al., 1997). Second, both the base rate and the effect size or model performance estimate should pertain to a clinically relevant population in which diagnostic, treatment, or risk decisions would actually be made. For example, comparing individuals with a history of suicide attempts with healthy controls (a common study design) could be meaningfully applied in predicting suicide risk in the general population, where the 12-month prevalence of suicide attempts is extremely low (0.3%) (Borges et al., 2010), but this does not represent a clinically realistic use case. A more realistic scenario would involve predicting suicide risk in a psychiatric population presenting for clinical care, where the base rate would be higher, but could also vary with local triage and referral patterns. Evaluating prediction in this context would require an effect size or model performance estimate derived using controls from that same psychiatric population rather than healthy controls from the general population.

Determining an appropriate decision threshold (pt) differs from the other inputs because it is not primarily a property of the data or the model. It represents the predicted risk at which a specific clinical action becomes preferable and therefore encodes the relative consequences of false-positive and false-negative decisions (Vickers and Elkin, 2006). Because these consequences can vary across settings, resource constraints, and patient preferences, there is rarely a single universally appropriate value. In our examples, we focused on one illustrative threshold to make PPV, sensitivity, and Net Benefit concrete and to keep the narrative clear, but DCA would generally involve considering a range of clinically plausible thresholds (Van Calster et al., 2018; Vickers et al., 2019).

sec.title: 4.2 High-risk populations: predictive value and population coverage
sec.p: Given how strongly low base rates can constrain predictive value and clinical utility, a natural response is to focus the development of prediction models on high-risk subgroups. However, identifying such subgroups is itself a multistep classification problem involving referral, screening, and clinical assessment, each with its own sensitivity and specificity limitations. Cases missed at any earlier stage become false negatives of the overall identification process and are absent from performance estimates calculated only within the final high-risk group. This is well illustrated by our example of psychosis risk prediction: while predicting who will transition to psychosis within the CHR cohort benefits from a relatively high 19% 24-month transition rate (De Pablo et al., 2021), the CHR criteria themselves have low sensitivity, identifying only 6.7% of people who will later develop psychosis (Talukder et al., 2025). Strong performance within a high-risk subpopulation may therefore give an overly optimistic impression of the likely clinical impact if most eventual cases are missed before the prediction model is even applied. Accordingly, given that our goal is to maximize clinical impact rather than merely predictive performance, the development of prediction models should be guided by an assessment of where the main bottlenecks lie across the full clinical pathway, not just the final prediction stage within the high-risk group.

sec.title: 4.3 Discriminative vs. causal effect sizes
sec.p: Discriminative effects, which reflect individual or group differences (e.g., patients vs. controls), and causal effects, which quantify the impact of an intervention (e.g., treatment vs. placebo), are often conflated (Shmueli, 2010; Ramspek et al., 2021; Dyer, 2025). E2P Simulator was designed for interpreting only discriminative effects, which are relevant for building prediction models. For interpreting causal effect sizes (Kraemer and Kupfer, 2006), other interactive tools are already available: https://rpsychologist.com/cohend.

sec.title: 4.4 No single metric tells the whole story
sec.p: While in this paper we have highlighted the limitations of ROC-AUC and the informativeness of PR-AUC and Net Benefit for assessing translational value, it is important to note that all metrics come with trade-offs (Van Calster et al., 2025). For example, although the invariance of ROC-AUC to base rates can obscure a model’s actual translational value, this same property makes it valuable for benchmarking discriminative ability across different contexts. Furthermore, while both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC provide convenient summary measures of performance across the entire range of classification thresholds, only a small range of those thresholds may be clinically relevant. Net Benefit, on the other hand, does require specifying clinically relevant thresholds but that is not always easy to do for non-clinical experts and may also vary based on patients’ preferences or resource constraints, leading to inaccurate NB estimates (Rousson and Zumbrunn, 2011; Lord et al., 2019). Finally, rank-based metrics like ROC-AUC and PR-AUC provide information only about relative risk. This does not guarantee that the absolute risk estimates are accurate and match observed probabilities - this is known as calibration (Van Calster et al., 2019); while we did not address it in this paper, E2P Simulator does include a module allowing researchers to explore how changes in measurement reliability and base rates may affect calibration (see Section 5.5 for a more detailed discussion). Overall, a robust evaluation requires a multi-faceted approach, combining multiple complementary metrics and visualization tools. This comprehensive perspective is exactly what E2P Simulator was designed to facilitate.

sec.title: 5.1 Normality assumptions and idealized distributions
sec.p: The classification examples presented in this paper rely on Gaussian approximations: binary outcome mode assumes that the predictor or model score is normally distributed within each outcome group, whereas continuous outcome mode assumes a bivariate normal distribution of the predictor and outcome. These assumptions are necessary because commonly reported metrics such as Cohen’s d, Pearson’s r, and ROC-AUC summarize effect magnitude or discrimination but do not determine the shapes of the underlying distributions. Thus, when using these as inputs, E2P Simulator reconstructs distributions consistent with those values under Gaussian assumptions, even though clinical and behavioral data may often be skewed or heavy-tailed (Loth et al., 2021). Binormal models can approximate overall discrimination reasonably well across a range of distributional forms (Hanley, 1988; Hajian-Tilaki et al., 1997), but departures from normality may have greater effects on the ROC curve and threshold-specific metrics (Walsh, 1997). The numerical results obtained with E2P Simulator should therefore be treated as approximations when the empirical distributions are unknown or non-Gaussian. Although E2P Simulator v1.3.0 does not support non-Gaussian distributions, predictive utility analysis itself does not rely on parametric assumptions and could be performed by simply resampling the observed score distributions under different measurement noise and base rate assumptions, providing more exact estimates. Future releases of E2P Simulator will support this functionality.

sec.title: 5.2 Uncertainty around input estimates
sec.p: E2P Simulator currently treats provided inputs as point estimates and does not propagate uncertainty in effect size, measurement reliability, or outcome base rate. Researchers can examine the consequences of uncertainty by simply repeating the analysis across confidence limits or other plausible values. Automated propagation of uncertainty across multiple inputs may be incorporated in future versions of E2P Simulator.

sec.title: 5.3 Interaction effects in multivariable models
sec.p: The multivariable model simulations that we presented in this paper do not account for non-linear relationships or interaction effects that machine learning models are designed to capitalize on. However, empirical evidence suggests this limitation may be less critical than may be expected. A systematic review by Christodoulou et al. (2019) showed that complex machine learning models rarely outperform simpler logistic regression in clinical prediction. Similarly, Schulz et al. (2020) found that deep learning models did not outperform simple linear models as sample size increased in UK Biobank brain-imaging data (with more recent work suggesting that this may be due to the disproportionate effect of measurement unreliability on interaction effects (Schulz and Ritter, 2026)). Finally, some research fields, like genetics, are primarily relying on linear models to begin with (Hill, 2010). Thus, while we may expect all kinds of interaction effects among our predictors to exist, they appear to contribute modestly to overall predictive performance in most clinical contexts.

sec.title: 5.4 Time to event prediction, multiclass prediction, stratification, subtypes
sec.p: While E2P Simulator currently focuses on binary classification and dichotomized continuous outcomes, it does not yet cover several important prediction contexts, including multiclass classification (e.g., subtyping, differential diagnosis, differential treatment response), risk stratification, time-to-event prediction, and longitudinal or trajectory modeling. Nevertheless, the same fundamental challenges stemming from measurement reliability and outcome base rate limitations remain equally critical in these scenarios.

sec.title: 5.5 Calibration
sec.p: One important aspect of clinical prediction modeling that we have not addressed in this paper is calibration (Van Calster et al., 2019; Steyerberg et al., 2010; Collins et al., 2025). Unlike discrimination metrics such as ROC-AUC, which assess a model’s ability to rank individuals by relative risk, calibration evaluates the accuracy of absolute risk estimates. A model is well-calibrated when the predicted probabilities correspond to the observed event frequencies across the range of predicted risks—for example, when patients predicted to have a 20% risk of an event experience it about 20% of the time. Calibration is essential for clinical decision-making because absolute risk determines the decision threshold (pt) at which net benefit (ΔNB) is computed.

Calibration can be influenced by both measurement reliability and outcome base rate. Low reliability broadens predictor distributions and can flatten the calibration slope, while shifts in base rate between settings can systematically bias predicted probabilities upward or downward. Consequently, calibration is especially critical to evaluate in deployment conditions, where both base rates and measurement properties often differ from those in the development dataset. E2P Simulator includes an interactive visualization to explore these influences.

sec.title: Data availability
sec.p: This work presents a statistical tool and does not involve empirical data. The source code for E2P Simulator is openly available at https://github.com/povilaskarvelis/e2p-simulator under the MIT license. An archived version is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21839127.

sec.title: Supplementary note 1: statistical models for binary and continuous outcome modes
sec.p: This note describes the statistical framework underlying the calculations performed by the main dashboard of E2P Simulator v1.3.0.

sec.title: 1.1.1 Score distributions and measurement reliability
sec.p:
Binary outcome mode uses a binormal model for a latent, error-free predictor or model score X* and a binary outcome Y (Metz, 1978; Hanley and McNeil, 1982). Before measurement error is introduced, the score distributions are
X*|Y=0~𝒩(0,1), X*|Y=1~𝒩(dtrue,1),
(1)

where dtrue is the error-free standardized mean difference (Cohen’s d) between the positive and negative outcome classes. The simulator’s true view uses these latent score distributions, while the observed view incorporates measurement error through the observed score X :
X|Y=0~𝒩(0,1ICC1), X|Y=1~𝒩(dtrueaκ,1ICC2),
(2)

where aκ=sin[(π/2)κ]. Here, ICC1 and ICC2 are the intraclass correlation coefficients describing predictor reliability in the negative and positive groups, respectively, and Cohen’s κ is the chance-corrected agreement coefficient used to represent the reliability of the binary outcome labels. The attenuation factor aκ equals one under perfect outcome-label reliability and decreases as κ declines. Consequently, lower predictor reliability widens the observed score distributions, while lower outcomelabel reliability reduces their mean separation. The relationship between κ and the reliability of an underlying continuous classification variable follows the population model described by Kraemer (1979). To standardize this attenuated mean difference when the observed group variances differ, the simulator divides by the root mean square of their standard deviations:
dobserved=dtrueak12(ICC1−1+ICC2−1)=dtrue2ICC1ICC2ICC1+ICC2sin(π2κ).
(3)

This is the attenuation relationship used in the main text (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025). The resulting dobserved is Cohen’s d when the two observed within-group variances are equal and the nonpooled standardized mean difference denoted by d* below when they differ.

sec.title: 1.1.2 Classification metrics and ROC-AUC
sec.p:
For either the true or observed view, let the selected negative and positive score distributions have means μ0, μ1 and standard deviations σ0, σ1. For an upper-tail score threshold t, the false-positive and true-positive rates are
FPR(t)=1−Φ(t−μ0σ0),
(4)
TPR(t)=1−Φ(t−μ1σ1),
(5)

where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Sensitivity is TPR(t) and specificity is 1 – FPR(t). The corresponding population proportions, rather than sample counts, in the four cells of the confusion matrix are
TP=ϕ TPR, FN=ϕ(1−TPR), FP=(1−ϕ)FPR, TN=(1−ϕ)(1−FPR).
(6)
where the positive-outcome base rate is denoted by ϕ = P(Y = 1).

All threshold-specific metrics are calculated from these quantities. In particular, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) are
PPV(t)=ϕTPR(t)ϕTPR(t)+(1−ϕ)FPR(t),
(7)
NPV(t)=(1−ϕ)[1−FPR(t)](1−ϕ)[1−FPR(t)]+ϕ[1−TPR(t)].
(8)

The other primary dashboard metrics are accuracy, balanced accuracy, the F1 score, and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC):
Accuracy=TP+TN,
(9)
Balanced Accuracy=TPR+1−FPR2,
(10)
F1=2PPV TPRPPV+TPR,
(11)
MCC=TPTN−FPFN(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN).
(12)

Moving t across the score range gives the ROC curve. Under the binormal model,
ROC-AUC=P(X1>X0)=Φ(μ1−μ0σ02+σ12)=Φ(d*2),
(13)
where X1 and X0 are independent scores from the positive and negative groups and d* = (μ1 – μ0)/(σ02+σ12)/2 (Hanley and McNeil, 1982; Ruscio, 2008). With equal variances, d* reduces to Cohen’s d.

The precision–recall curve is obtained from PPV(t) and TPR(t) over the same thresholds (Davis and Goadrich, 2006; Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015). For precision–recall points (Ri, Pi) ordered by increasing recall, where Ri is recall (TPR) and Pi is precision (PPV), PR-AUC is calculated using the trapezoidal rule:
PR-AUC≈∑i(Ri−Ri−1)Pi+Pi−12.
(14)

In binary mode, changing ϕ changes the relative frequency of positive and negative outcomes while leaving the class-conditional score distributions—the score distributions within the two outcome groups— unchanged. It therefore changes PPV, NPV, PR-AUC, and Net Benefit but not the ROC curve. Using this reweighting to represent another population assumes a prior-probability shift: sensitivity and specificity at each threshold are expected to remain the same in that population (Brabec et al., 2020).

sec.title: 1.1.3 Effect-size conversions, probability thresholds, and Net Benefit
sec.p:
To express d* using other commonly reported effect-size measures, binary mode converts it to the log odds ratio log(OR) (and hence the odds ratio), the point-biserial correlation rpb, Cohen’s U3, and η2:
log(OR)=πd*3, rpb=d*(d*)2+[ϕ(1−ϕ)]−1, U3=Φ(d*), η2=rpb2.
(15)

The log odds-ratio conversion uses a logistic-distribution approximation, while rpb also incorporates the base rate ϕ (Chinn, 2000; McGrath and Meyer, 2006). The U3 interpretation and the relationship between a standardized mean difference and rpb assume equal within-group variances. When the group reliabilities differ, applying these conversions to d* provides standardized effect-size summaries, while the ROC and precision-recall curves are calculated directly from the two modeled distributions.

These effect sizes summarize separation across the full score range, whereas classification additionally requires a score threshold t. E2P parameterizes this cutoff using the decision threshold probability pt, the predicted risk at which the specified action becomes preferable given the relative consequences of false-positive and false-negative decisions. To link pt to t, the posterior event probability conditional on a score x is obtained from Bayes’ theorem (Fischer, 2021):
P(Y=1|X=x)=ϕf1(x)ϕf1(x)+(1−ϕ)f0(x),
(16)

where f1 and f0 are the two normal densities. The displayed threshold probability is therefore pt = P (Y =1 | X = t) under the assumed model. Writing logit(p) = log[p/(1 – p)], the corresponding score threshold is obtained by solving
logit(pt)=logit(ϕ)+log(σ0σ1)−(t−μ1)2σ12+(t−μ0)22σ02.
(17)

When σ0 = σ1 = σ and μ1 ≠ μ0, this gives the unique mapping
t=μ0+μ12+σ2μ1−μ0[logit(pt)−logit(ϕ)].
(18)

If μ1 = μ0 under equal variances, the two class-conditional distributions are identical, the predicted probability remains ϕ at every score, and no unique threshold exists. When the variances differ, the equation is quadratic and a probability may correspond to two score values or to none; the simulator retains a single upper-tail classification rule and uses the solution on the branch where predicted probability increases with the score.

Once t and pt are linked, Net Benefit provides a decision-analytic measure that combines the resulting true- and false-positive rates as defined by Vickers and Elkin (2006); Vickers et al. (2019):
NB(t,pt)=ϕTPR(t)−(1−ϕ)FPR(t)pt1−pt.
(19)

The odds pt/(1 – pt) determine the relative penalty assigned to false-positive classifications. A higher pt penalizes false positives more heavily and therefore favors specificity, while a lower pt favors sensitivity. The reference strategies of classifying everyone as positive (“all”) and classifying everyone as negative (“none”) are
N Ball(pt)=ϕ−(1−ϕ)pt1−pt, N Bnone(pt)=0.
(20)

For each pt, the decision curve shows the largest Net Benefit available along the modeled ROC curve, N Bmodel(pt) = maxs N B(s, pt), where s ranges over score thresholds. The red marker instead evaluates the currently selected score threshold t. Its incremental Net Benefit is
ΔN B=N B(t,pt)−max{N Ball(pt),N Bnone(pt)}.
(21)
A positive ΔNB indicates that the selected threshold provides greater Net Benefit than both reference strategies.

sec.title: 1.2.1 Bivariate-normal model and measurement reliability
sec.p:
Continuous outcome mode begins with a continuous predictor X and continuous outcome Y ; the outcome is dichotomized only when classification metrics are calculated. The standardized variables are modeled using a bivariate-normal distribution with Pearson correlation r:
(XY)~𝒩2[(00),(1rr1)].
(22)

The true view uses r = rtrue, whereas the observed view applies the classical attenuation relationship (Spearman, 1904)
robserved=rtrueICCxICCy.
(23)

Here, ICCx and ICCy are the intraclass correlation coefficients describing the reliability of the predictor and outcome. Because both views retain standardized marginal distributions, measurement error is represented by attenuation of their correlation, with corresponding variance explained R2 = r2 . This formulation assumes that the reliabilities summarize random measurement error in the predictor and outcome and that these errors are independent of each other and of the true scores.

To obtain classification metrics, the simulator defines the positive class as the upper ϕ proportion of the continuous outcome. Because Y is standardized, the corresponding cutoff is
c=Φ−1(1−ϕ),
(24)

with Y > c classified as positive. Consequently, changing ϕ in continuous mode changes the outcome cutoff and the resulting class-conditional predictor distributions, rather than simply reweighting fixed groups.

sec.title: 1.2.2 Classification after dichotomizing the outcome
sec.p:
At an upper-tail predictor threshold t, the true-positive and false-positive rates are P (X > t | Y > c) and P(X > t | Y ≤ c), respectively. Under the bivariate-normal model for a dichotomized continuous outcome (Tate, 1955), X | Y = y ~ 𝒩(ry, 1 – r2), giving
TPR(t)=1ϕ∫c∞[1−Φ(t−ry1−r2)]φ(y)dy,
(25)
FPR(t)=11−ϕ∫−∞c[1−Φ(t−ry1−r2)]φ(y)dy,
(26)

where φ is the standard normal density. The confusion-matrix proportions and all derived prediction metrics are then calculated as in binary mode. To express the decision threshold on the probability scale used throughout the simulator, we calculate the probability of the positive outcome Y > c conditional on a predictor score X = t. Because Y | X = t ~ 𝒩(rt, 1 – r2), this probability is
P(Y>c|X=t)=1−Φ(c−rt1−r2).
(27)

Solving P(Y > c | X = t) = pt for t, when r = 0, gives
t=c−1−r2Φ−1(1−pt)r.
(28)
When r = 0, X and Y are independent under the bivariate-normal model, so the predicted probability remains ϕ at every score and no unique score threshold exists.

The one-dimensional integrals for TPR and FPR are evaluated numerically using trapezoidal quadrature. Evaluating them across a range of score thresholds produces the ROC and precision–recall curves, whose areas are also obtained by trapezoidal integration. The numerical integration limits extend at least eight standard deviations into each outcome tail. Net Benefit and ΔNB are calculated from these threshold-specific sensitivity and specificity values using the same definitions as in binary mode.

sec.title: 1.2.3 Induced group differences
sec.p:
To report continuous-mode results using the same group-difference effect sizes as binary mode, the simulator calculates the class-conditional distributions of X induced by dichotomizing Y. Using subscripts 1 and 0 for the positive and negative groups, respectively, and writing h = φ(c), their means and variances follow from standard truncated-normal results (Tallis, 1961):
μ1=E(X|Y>c)=rhϕ, μ0=E(X|Y≤c)=−rh1−ϕ,
(29)
σ12=(1−r2)+r2[1+chϕ−(hϕ)2], σ02=(1−r2)+r2[1+ch1−ϕ−(h1−ϕ)2].
(30)

The simulator uses these moments to report a prevalence-weighted standardized mean difference d, the non-pooled standardized mean difference d*, Glass’s Δ, and the rank-biserial correlation rrb:
d=μ1−μ0(1−ϕ)σ02+ϕσ12,
(31)
d*=μ1−μ0(σ02+σ12)/2,
(32)
Glass's Δ=μ1−μ0σ0, rrb=2ROC-AUC−1.
(33)

The d* value is used for the displayed U3, odds ratio, log odds ratio, and point-biserial correlation through the same conversions given above. Because the two groups are created by truncating a continuous outcome, their predictor distributions are not generally normal. The moments above are used for the displayed effect-size summaries, while ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and the threshold-specific metrics are calculated directly from the bivariate-normal model.

Within these distributional and reliability models, a standardized effect size or correlation, together with the specified reliability, base rate, and decision threshold, defines a complete set of expected prediction metrics. The results are population-level scenario estimates under the stated assumptions. Empirical score distributions can yield different ROC and precision–recall curves even when they share the same Cohen’s d, Pearson’s r, or ROC-AUC.

sec.title: Supplementary note 2: combining multiple predictors
sec.p: E2P Simulator v1.3.0 includes calculators that estimate the combined predictive performance of multiple predictors from their individual associations with the outcome and their degree of collinearity.

For a binary outcome, the combined separation between the two groups can be summarized by Mahalanobis D, a multidimensional version of Cohen’s d. Given p predictors with Cohen’s d values d1, d2, ... , dp and a correlation matrix R describing their collinearity, Mahalanobis D is (Mahalanobis, 1936; Del Giudice, 2009):
D2=dTR−1d
(34)

where d = (d1, d2, ..., dp)┬. To keep the calculator simple, we assume that all predictors have the same effect size (d1 = d2 = ··· = dp = d) and the same level of collinearity. In the calculator, collinearity is represented by a common pairwise correlation, denoted by ρ. This gives:
D=dp1+(p−1)ρ.
(35)

The numerator reflects the number of predictors, while the denominator adjusts for shared information. When the predictors are uncorrelated (ρ = 0), each adds new information and D=dp. When they are perfectly correlated (ρ = 1), they are completely redundant and D = d, regardless of how many predictors are added.

We can then convert D to ROC-AUC using the same relationship as for Cohen’s d:
ROC-AUC=Φ(D2)
(36)

where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Substituting the simplified D gives:
ROC-AUC=Φ(dp2{1+(p−1)ρ}).
(37)

This conversion assumes that the predictors are approximately normally distributed within each group and have similar variability and correlation patterns in both groups. After setting the outcome base rate, the simulator also calculates PR-AUC. The relationship between ROC-AUC and PR-AUC depends on these assumptions as well as the base rate.

The same logic applies to continuous outcomes. In the general case, the variance explained by a linear combination of predictors is:
R2=ryXTRXX−1ryX.
(38)

Here, ryX contains the correlations between each predictor and the outcome, and RXX describes collinearity among the predictors. If every predictor has the same correlation r with the outcome and the same collinearity ρ, the formula simplifies to:
R2=pr21+(p−1)ρ.
(39)

This formula captures the same intuition: adding predictors helps most when each one contributes information that the others do not already contain. Any combination of p, r, and ρ must produce a valid value between 0 and 1 for R2.

To express this continuous-outcome result as ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, the simulator assumes a bivariate normal distribution for the predictor and continuous outcome, then splits the outcome at the cutoff that gives the chosen base rate and calculates the classification metrics. PR-AUC is obtained by trapezoidal numerical integration. This is useful for studying outcomes that are often reported as categories, such as treatment response versus non-response, but different outcome distributions or cutoffs could give different results.

These formulas describe additive linear models and do not include interactions or other non-linear relationships. This is a useful starting point because, in many clinical prediction studies, complex models have not consistently outperformed logistic regression or other linear models (Christodoulou et al., 2019; Schulz et al., 2020); linear models are also standard in fields such as quantitative genetics (Hill, 2010). Even when real-world predictors vary in strength and collinearity, the general trends (e.g., diminishing returns with correlated predictors) remain informative for research planning.
In the main text we consider two examples to demonstrate the use of each multivariable calculator (Supp. Fig. 1 and Supp. Fig. 2).

body.p: This important work outlines why commonly applied performance metrics in predictive modelling do not accurately reflect translational potential, using the example of psychiatric care; it provides a web-based tool to contextualize effect sizes in psychiatry with respect to reliability and base rates, and to calculate the real-world utility of prediction models under different scenarios. The evidence supporting the conclusions is convincing, incorporating established psychometric principles that will be of use for multiple fields, along with transparent quantitative logic and example applications. The work will be of broad interest to both clinical experts and scientists in biomedicine and the life sciences.

The authors have adequately addressed my previous comments.
Summary:

This important work provides a web-based tool to contextualize effect sizes in psychiatry with respect to reliability and base rates (collectively referred to as predictive utility analysis). The methods for the tool incorporate established psychometric principles that I think are of use for multiple fields in this seemingly easy to use tool. I agree with the critical importance of this tool and the methodological points made in this manuscript. Enthusiasm for the manuscript has been strengthened through revision by increased clarity on the formulation of the paper and stated goals of the examples used. The use of this tool will likely bring forth additional thoughts, but I commend the authors on their work and helping to better disseminate these ideas, while also acknowledging some of the remaining areas for further development.

Likewise, users of E2P should remain vigilant to distinctions between predictive utility and validity. As current construed, however, these minor weaknesses do not substantively undermine my enthusiasm or estimate of the impact of this work.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

We would like to thank the editors and reviewers for taking the time to provide thoughtful comments on our manuscript. We were delighted to receive positive feedback, and we believe that the revisions made in response to these comments helped strengthen our manuscript even more. The key changes to the manuscript include:
(1) Predictive utility analysis is now a more central focus of the paper, providing more guidance and discussion for how to apply it beyond the presented examples.
(2) The details, assumptions, and limitations of the statistical settings explored by E2P Simulator are now discussed much more extensively.

(3) The worked examples have been refined and updated. Each example now states its inputs, target population, and decision threshold with more detailed reasoning, in line with the guidance in Section 4.1. Several reported values in the treatment response, suicide risk, and Alzheimer's biomarker examples have also been updated as a result, although it did not change the overall conclusions and insights.
(4) In the meantime, E2P Simulator has also been updated to v1.3.0, which now includes:
a) Analytical solutions for the continuous outcome scenarios, which were sampling-based before. This provides more precise results for the treatment response prediction example.
b) Threshold probability, pt, can now be set by entering a numerical value (previously, it was only possible to do it by sliding the threshold itself), which improves the ease of use.
c) An interactive tutorial that explains the interface of E2P Simulator, making the interface more intuitive.
Below we provide answers to each comment and quote the revised parts of the manuscript.
