Relatedly, the analytical context and the methodological assumptions are not clearly specified. Many arguments and demonstrations are derived in univariate, group-comparison settings and then discussed in a way that can be read as broadly applicable.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and for highlighting these weaknesses. We now provide a lot more guidance on selecting the right base rate, and we also discuss the assumptions and limitations of the statistical settings under consideration in more detail.
Regarding the base rate, we now expand on it in a newly added Section 4.1 Selecting appropriate inputs for predictive utility analysis:

“Disease prevalence estimates can also vary substantially with study design, geographic region, cohort composition, and estimation method (e.g., Simeone et al., 2015; Flor et al., 2020). When base rates are very low, obtaining precise estimates becomes especially difficult (McGrath and Burke, 2024). For predictive utility analysis to be informative, two considerations are essential. First, the selected base rate must correspond to the population represented by the effect size or model performance estimate, because these quantities are not independent (Leeflang et al., 2013, 2009; Moons et al., 1997). Second, both the base rate and the effect size or model performance estimate should pertain to a clinically relevant population in which diagnostic, treatment, or risk decisions would actually be made. For example, comparing individuals with a history of suicide attempts with healthy controls (a common study design) could be meaningfully applied in predicting suicide risk in the general population, where the 12month prevalence of suicide attempts is extremely low (0.3%) (Borges et al., 2010), but this does not represent a clinically realistic use case. A more realistic scenario would involve predicting suicide risk in a psychiatric population presenting for clinical care, where the base rate would be higher, but could also vary with local triage and referral patterns. Evaluating prediction in this context would require an effect size or model performance estimate derived using controls from that same psychiatric population rather than healthy controls from the general population.”
We also highlight these base rate selection nuances in a newly introduced Box 1, which provides a high-level summary of the predictive utility analysis workflow:

“Use the outcome base rate expected where the predictor or model will be applied, rather than the proportion of cases in the study sample. The target population and, for risk prediction, the time horizon should align with those used to estimate the observed effect.”
We also make these considerations more explicit in the examples we provide, eg, in section 3.1.1 we say:

“Finally, because the effect size in question summarizes the differences between patients and healthy controls, the relevant target population for this illustrative analysis is the general population. Recent national surveys estimate depression prevalence to be around 9.2% among Americans aged 12 years or older (Goodwin et al., 2022) and 7.7% among Canadians aged 15 years or older (Halladay et al., 2026). We therefore use 8% as a rounded illustrative base rate within this range. Note that a more clinically realistic scenario, such as those explored below, would consider the biomarker in a preselected, higher prevalence group (e.g., help-seeking individuals); however, evaluating the biomarker in this setting would require an effect size estimated using controls drawn from that same target population rather than healthy controls from the general population.”

As for the statistical setting and its limitations, we address this directly in the expanded Limitations section. Section 5.1 now states the distributional assumptions behind the binary classification examples:

“The classification examples presented in this paper rely on Gaussian approximations: binary outcome mode assumes that the predictor or model score is normally distributed within each outcome group, whereas continuous outcome mode assumes a bivariate normal distribution of the predictor and outcome. These assumptions are necessary because commonly reported metrics such as Cohen’s d, Pearson’s r, and ROC-AUC summarize effect magnitude or discrimination but do not determine the shapes of the underlying distributions. Thus, when using these as inputs, E2P Simulator reconstructs distributions consistent with those values under Gaussian assumptions, even though clinical and behavioral data may often be skewed or heavy-tailed (Loth et al., 2021). Binormal models can approximate overall discrimination reasonably well across a range of distributional forms (Hanley, 1988; Hajian-Tilaki et al., 1997), but departures from normality may have greater effects on the ROC curve and thresholdspecific metrics (Walsh, 1997). The numerical results obtained with E2P Simulator should therefore be treated as approximations when the empirical distributions are unknown or nonGaussian. Although E2P Simulator v1.3.0 does not support non-Gaussian distributions, predictive utility analysis itself does not rely on parametric assumptions and could be performed by simply resampling the observed score distributions under different measurement noise and base rate assumptions, providing more exact estimates. Future releases of E2P Simulator will support this functionality.”
In Section 5.3 we now address the assumptions behind the multivariable demonstrations:

“The multivariable model simulations that we presented in this paper do not account for nonlinear relationships or interaction effects that machine learning models are designed to capitalize on. However, empirical evidence suggests this limitation may be less critical than may be expected. A systematic review by Christodoulou et al. (2019) showed that complex machine learning models rarely outperform simpler logistic regression in clinical prediction. Similarly, Schulz et al. (2020) found that deep learning models did not outperform simple linear models as sample size increased in UK Biobank brain-imaging data (with more recent work suggesting that this may be due to the disproportionate effect of measurement unreliability on interaction effects (Schulz and Ritter, 2026)). Finally, some research fields, like genetics, are primarily relying on linear models to begin with (Hill, 2010). Thus, while we may expect all kinds of interaction effects among our predictors to exist, they appear to contribute modestly to overall predictive performance in most clinical contexts.”
In Section 5.4 we now specify the prediction settings that the current implementation does not cover:

“While E2P Simulator currently focuses on binary classification and dichotomized continuous outcomes, it does not yet cover several important prediction contexts, including multiclass classification (e.g., subtyping, differential diagnosis, differential treatment response), risk stratification, time-to-event prediction, and longitudinal or trajectory modeling. Nevertheless, the same fundamental challenges stemming from measurement reliability and outcome base rate limitations remain equally critical in these scenarios.”

We have also expanded the discussion around base rates in a newly added Section 4.2, which provides some considerations and observations around the high-risk subpopulations as a way to address low base rate challenges:
“4.2. High-risk populations: predictive value and population coverage

Given how strongly low base rates can constrain predictive value and clinical utility, a natural response is to focus the development of prediction models on high-risk subgroups. However, identifying such subgroups is itself a multistep classification problem involving referral, screening, and clinical assessment, each with its own sensitivity and specificity limitations. Cases missed at any earlier stage become false negatives of the overall identification process and are absent from performance estimates calculated only within the final high-risk group. This is well illustrated by our example on psychosis risk prediction: while predicting who will transition to psychosis within the CHR cohort benefits from a relatively high 19% 24-month transition rate (Salazar de Pablo et al., 2021), CHR criteria itself have low sensitivity, identifying only 6.7% of people who will later develop psychosis (Talukder et al., 2025). Strong performance within a high-risk subpopulation may therefore give an overly optimistic impression of the likely clinical impact if most eventual cases are missed before the prediction model is even applied. Accordingly, given that our goal is to maximize clinical impact rather than merely predictive performance, the development of prediction models should be guided by an assessment of where the main bottlenecks lie across the full clinical pathway, not just the final prediction stage within the high-risk group.”

body.p: Thank you for raising this concern, which goes to the heart of the paper’s contribution. The JOSS article (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025b) is a two-page software paper: it announces the existence of the tool, states its dependencies and licence, and points to the repository. It contains no derivations, no worked examples, no guidance on the selection of inputs, and no discussion of the assumptions or limitations of the underlying statistical model. The online how-to guide provides more details and context but is a distilled version of the core motivations, assumptions and guidance. This manuscript (especially the current revised version) provides a much more detailed and literature-supported argument for the need of predictive utility analysis, guidance on how to perform it correctly, as well as a detailed discussion of caveats and broader considerations. Most importantly, the current manuscript goes beyond E2P Simulator and is focused more generally on predictive utility analysis as a principled workflow for evaluating findings and planning studies (with E2P Simulator being an accessible interactive tool for performing such analysis).

This important work provides a web-based tool to contextualize effect sizes in psychiatry with respect to reliability and base rates (collectively referred to as predictive utility analysis). The methods for the tool incorporate established psychometric principles that I think are of use for multiple fields in this seemingly easy-to-use tool. I agree with the critical importance of this tool and the methodological points made in this manuscript. Enthusiasm for the manuscript is weakened by a lack of clarity on the formulation of the paper and stated goals of the examples used, with the inferences and impact on clinical decision making from various parameterizations via this tool left open-ended.
Strengths:

This paper presents a well-considered and, what I think will be highly useful, web-based tool to contextualize effect sizes with respect to reliability and base rates. As the authors rightly point out, such a tool could be used in conjunction with widespread analytic power analysis tools in study planning. The paper also well contexualizes the need for such a tool in the relatively recent history of concerns of power, reliability, and inference in psychiatry specifically, and more general meta-scientific debates in psychology and neuroscience.
Weaknesses:

My primary feedback on this manuscript is the lack of clarity in what the paper itself, specifically, separate from the tool, is hoping to achieve. There is a central, but unresolved, tension in whether the reader is supposed to:
(1) focus on the specifics of the examples used and whether to reevaluate the substantive claims from the studies,
(2) buy in to how various reliability and base rate parameters impact modeling outcomes,
(3) receive an introduction to the tool itself.

In my estimation, the largest contribution to the field here is in (2) and (3), but currently much of the real estate of the paper is dedicated to several examples of (1). While these specific examples may be illustrative to some degree, I think given the number and brevity of such, they are unlikely to incidentally achieve points (2) and (3) above. Specific examples include the assertion of kappas for DSM diagnoses, without much nuance (e.g., see https://psycnet.apa.org/buy/2015-27500-001). Given the relatively limited space given to this example, however, it's hard to be entirely certain what the reviewer should take away.

A second point of concern is where this tool would be situated in the research pipeline. I agree with the authors that this tool could be used in ways that parallel power analysis. With that in mind, it seems the most common use of this tool for an individual investigator is likely to be in a priori study planning. In contrast, and with my point above in mind, the use of the tool for existing results is likely best done with multiple estimates of effect sizes, reliability, and base rates, as is common in meta-analysis or consensus reviews. Nevertheless, there is no real example or guidance around how this influences new study planning.

body.p: We are grateful for the reviewer’s careful and constructive assessment. This comment guided a substantial reframing of the paper: now in addition to the examples we put a lot more emphasis on the predictive utility analysis itself and provide more guidance on how to perform it, including what caveats need to be considered when selecting appropriate inputs.
The updated abstract now reads:

“… Here we argue that one important contributor to this translational gap is a pervasive misalignment between routine statistical analytic practices and the requirements for real-world decision making. To help address this, we introduce predictive utility analysis: a statistical workflow for estimating the practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by accounting for outcome base rates and measurement reliability. Starting from effect size or model performance estimates, the workflow simulates expected real-world performance in a target population and summarizes it across complementary metrics including positive and negative predictive value, Precision-Recall AUC, and Net Benefit. Analogous to how power analysis is used for determining the conditions needed to achieve statistical significance, predictive utility analysis can help determine the conditions needed to achieve practical significance. We implement and illustrate this workflow using E2P Simulator, a recently developed open-source web tool that makes predictive utility analysis accessible through interactive simulations and publicationready visualizations…”
We have also updated the title to reflect this emphasis:
“Evaluating biomarkers and prediction models: predictive utility analysis with E2P Simulator”
We now also include Box 1, which summarizes the predictive utility analysis workflow without having to go through the detailed examples.

We have also introduced Section 4.1 for a detailed discussion on the nuances and caveats for selecting appropriate inputs for predictive utility analysis (see the revised manuscript for the full section). Among other things, this section also addresses your specific comment about DSM reliability estimates:

“For example, interrater reliability of DSM diagnoses computed from clinicians rating the same recorded interviews can be higher than estimates based on repeated independent interviews (Chmielewski et al., 2015); however, the latter is more relevant because it better reflects the reliability of repeated assessments in real-world contexts (Regier et al., 2013), and that is what we used in our examples.”

disp-quote.p: A third point is that more nuance would be useful in the introduction about the current state of psychiatry research. For example, I share many of the authors' concerns about reliability, power, reproducibility, and barriers to translation. That said, it is the case that while effect sizes should be considered considerably more, they are widely considered in psychiatry research via the common place of meta-analysis and other data pooling approaches. Another such example that the authors state in the context of reliability:

body.p: "However, this [reliability] attenuation is rarely accounted for in routine analyses in psychiatry". This is true in practice, but somewhat misleading insofar as the method by which to do this remains unclear. For example, should we all report disattenuated associations, assuming there is no error and everything is perfectly reliable? This, of course, would be unrealistic to expect zero error. That we can achieve this with the new tool is clear, but the nuance of how and under what circumstances it should be done is not clear, and such nuance should be better reflected in the framing of the problem. That is, there is also a lack of clarity on what ought to be best practices and field-wide goals, rather than simply the lack of an ability to model these factors.

Thank you for highlighting the need to further clarify these claims. Our argument is not that effect sizes are absent from psychiatric research or meta-analyses; it is that effect sizes, even when they are reported, are often difficult to interpret in an intuitive way. When it comes to poor reliability, the purpose of the predictive utility analysis is not to provide disattenuated values, but to show how much signal is lost (by comparing them to the observed and the disattenuated values). Another more general aim that we hope predictive utility analysis and this paper can help achieve is to increase the awareness of the importance of measurement reliability, prompting researchers to pay more attention to it, report it more consistently, and as a result of it, hopefully, find ways to improve it.
The Introduction now states:

“Even when effect sizes are reported and discussed (e.g., in meta-analyses), their meaningful interpretation often poses a problem (Funder and Ozer, 2019). The situation is further exacerbated by how effect sizes and thus their translational value are attenuated by measurement reliability, which often goes unassessed and unaddressed (Karvelis and Diaconescu, 2025a; Karvelis et al., 2023; Hedge et al., 2018).”
We now also state these points clearly in Section 2.5 when introducing Predictive utility analysis and E2P Simulator:

“To bring these statistical considerations together, we introduce predictive utility analysis: a statistical workflow for evaluating the practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by explicitly accounting for real-world outcome base rates, measurement reliability, and, where relevant, the decision threshold. The workflow can be thought of as consisting of two key components: (1) translating conventional effect size and model performance metrics into measures that more directly reflect expected predictive value and utility, including PPV, NPV, PR-AUC, and NB by accounting for real-world base rates and relevant clinical decision thresholds, and (2) determining how much performance is lost due to measurement reliability.”

disp-quote.p: Minor point

For conceptual clarity, it would benefit the manuscript to at least briefly mention the role of validity in translational importance. Of course, the current psychometric issues of reliability, base rate, power, etc are critical, but it should at least be mentioned, given the potential wide audience of this manuscript, validity is important as well. For example, highly reliable measures may not be valid indicators of underlying disease etiology (e.g., fMRI head motion is a highly reliable trait-level feature, but typically not considered an important predictor or consequence of mental health worth investing translational resources in). Relatedly, confounding as a general topic would be useful to mention just briefly, to help with the spirit of considering underlying issues in translation.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this distinction. Construct or etiological validity and predictive utility address different questions. The present framework asks what predictive value and clinical utility follow from observed group differences under specified assumptions about measurement reliability, outcome base rate, and decision threshold. Whether the predictor indexes disease etiology is not required for these calculations: predictors used for diagnosis, prognosis, or risk stratification may be useful without supporting an etiological interpretation, while etiological relevance does not itself establish predictive usefulness.

We have therefore kept a broader discussion of construct and etiological validity outside the scope of the manuscript. We have, however, added confounding to the new Section 4.1 because it can directly compromise the effect size or model performance estimates used as inputs to predictive utility analysis:

“Predictive utility analysis is informative only to the extent that its inputs are carefully and appropriately chosen. Effect sizes from individual studies are subject to sampling error and may be inflated by publication bias, selective reporting, or analytical flexibility (Button et al., 2013; Ioannidis, 2008; Ioannidis and Panagiotou, 2011). Similarly, estimates of multivariable model performance may be overly optimistic because of overfitting (e.g., Karvelis et al., 2022; Schnack and Kahn, 2016; Hunt et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025) or confounding features (Chyzhyk et al., 2022; Komeyer et al., 2025). This creates a tricky paradox: while our analysis shows that larger effect sizes are needed for clinical translation, many effects reported in the literature may already be inflated. To guard against these issues, researchers should use the most robust estimates available: effect sizes should ideally be supported by large samples, replication, or meta-analysis, while model performance should be estimated using properly held out or external validation data.”

disp-quote.p: I would like to thank the authors for their work. I truly appreciate their clear and structured definition of interpretative flaws in the current predictive psychiatry literature. The manuscript nevertheless has some issues in its current form, which, in my opinion, would need to be addressed.
Major

(1) The manuscript would substantially benefit from a paragraph introducing the common predictive modeling approach(es) to which the authors are referring. It seems there are a lot of implicit assumptions about the methodological details and nature of the predictive models which are not explicitly stated. Therefore, defining the methodological context would be helpful, specifically describing the common predictive model workflow, distributive assumptions, the statistical models which are used, etc. This might also be helpful in clearly distinguishing the statistical setting from related approaches, e.g., from crossvalidated machine-learning metrics, for which several of the metric mappings and conversions might not be valid or need to be calculated differently.

(2) In general, I would encourage the authors to nuance some of the stronger claims about what and in which cases predictive utility analysis and E2P can deliver. While the authors' use case is really important, it is nevertheless limited. For example, all conversions are derived under the assumption of (bi)variate normality and linear separability, which neglects that psychiatric and neuroimaging variables can be skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal and decision boundaries can be non-linear or even multi-variate. Similarly, section 3.3.2 is informative but currently reads as quite strong in its implications, given the simplifying assumptions behind the multivariable calculator (equal effect sizes, constant pairwise correlations, linear additivity).

Thus, while we may expect all kinds of interaction effects among our predictors to exist, they appear to contribute modestly to overall predictive performance in most clinical contexts.”
And highlight these simplifying assumptions when presenting multivariable simulation results in Section 3.1.2:

“E2P Simulator also includes multivariable calculators that estimate how many biomarkers of a given strength and collinearity would be required to achieve a specified performance target, assuming an additive linear model without interaction effects (see Supplementary note 2 for more details).”
And we have softened the language around its implications; in Section 3.2.2

“Because these predictors may capture overlapping information, collinearity can limit the incremental predictive gain obtained by combining them. For example, assuming an average collinearity of 0.15 among all predictors, we would need 20 predictors of r = 0.3 to achieve PRAUC = 0.8, which translates to R2 = 0.47 (Supplementary Fig. 2).”
In Section 5.4 we also explicitly highlight which statistical settings we have not covered in this paper:

“While E2P Simulator currently focuses on binary classification and dichotomized continuous outcomes, it does not yet cover several important prediction contexts, including multiclass classification (e.g., subtyping, differential diagnosis, differential treatment response), risk stratification, time-to-event prediction, and longitudinal or trajectory modeling. Nevertheless, the same fundamental challenges stemming from measurement reliability and outcome base rate limitations remain equally critical in these scenarios.”

disp-quote.p: (1) The sentence "The literature seems to be filled with weak and false positive findings (Ioannidis and Panagiotou, 2011; Collaboration, 2015; Ioannidis, 2005)" strikes me as unnecessarily strong, especially given that the cited work is at least a decade old. The case is already compelling without this sentence, and I recommend removing it. Moreover, I suggest avoiding implying that overfitting is unique to or inherent in ML approaches. Classical statistical modeling is subject to many of the same problems (e.g. data dredging, post-hoc variable selection, inadequate validation).

body.p: Thank you for this suggestion – we have removed the quoted sentence.
We also made sure that our discussion around overfitting is general enough to include all multivariable models, not only ML. Eg, in the Introduction we say:

“When multiple predictors of small effect sizes are then combined to build prediction models, they end up underperforming (which is often masked by inflated performance metrics due to overfitting).” And in Section 4.1 we now say:

“Similarly, estimates of multivariable model performance may be overly optimistic because of overfitting (e.g., Karvelis et al., 2022; Schnack and Kahn, 2016; Hunt et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025) or confounding features (Chyzhyk et al., 2022; Komeyer et al., 2025).”

disp-quote.p: (2) The explanation of ROC-AUC could be reframed for clarity, e.g "ROC-AUC can be interpreted as the probability that, given a randomly chosen positive and a randomly chosen negative individual, the model assigns a higher predicted risk score to the positive than to the negative." The phrase "ranks higher" without explicitly referring to the risk score may be confusing to some readers.

body.p: Thank you for suggesting a better phrasing. We have incorporated it; in Section 2.3.1:

“Calculating the area under ROC (ROC-AUC) provides an informative summary metric which captures the average probability that, given a randomly chosen positive and a randomly chosen negative individual (e.g., a patient with a psychiatric condition and a control), a predictor assigns a higher predicted risk score to the positive than to the negative.”

disp-quote.p: (3) In the depression biomarker example, the authors write: "Accounting for measurement reliability reveals that this observed effect would correspond to a much larger true effect, ..." The verb "accounting" here may be confusing, and does not reflect what is done: exploring via simulation how improved reliability would change effect sizes and predictive utility. I suggest reframing the sentence to make the intention clear.

(4) Relatedly, the phrase "simply improving measurement reliability" in line 260 underplays how difficult and resource-intensive it is to substantially improve reliability for many psychiatric measures. The word "simply" might not be warranted here.

body.p: Thank you for pointing these wording problems. We no longer use the word “accounting” and make it clear that we are simply exploring a hypothetical scenario where measurement reliability is higher. We also no longer say “simply improving” to not create a misleading interpretation that improving reliability is easy; in Section 3.1.1:

“We can then explore the consequences of a hypothetical improvement in measurement reliability. If both the biomarker and diagnostic outcome were measured perfectly, the expected effect would increase to d = 1.58, with substantially better predictive performance: ROC-AUC = 0.87, PR-AUC = 0.46, PPV = 0.34, sensitivity = 0.63, and ∆NB = 0.033 at pt = 0.15. This illustrates how much diagnostic prediction could improve through better measurement alone.”

disp-quote.p: (5) In the treatment-response section, the discussion of "neurocognitive predictors" and then "task-evoked BOLD signals" needs a better introduction, given that the reader has not read the paper the authors are referring to. Please specify what you mean by neurocognitive predictors (neuroimaging features, raw signals, task-fMRI derived response times or other metrics, cognitive test scores, clinical variables?). Moreover, from a clinical practice perspective, it would be important to at least acknowledge that taskbased fMRI is unlikely to become a routine clinical tool for antidepressant treatment selection in the foreseeable future.

body.p: We now clarify what we mean by neurocognitive predictors in Section 3.2.1:

“Research using multivariable / machine learning models suggests that neurocognitive predictors (brain activity and behavioral measures derived from cognitive tasks) can explain 20% of the variance (R² = 0.2) in symptom improvement in response to antidepressants and other treatments (Karvelis et al., 2022).”

Near-term routine use of task-based fMRI for treatment selection is indeed unlikely. The example is retained for a narrower methodological purpose: it asks what the reported performance of this published predictor class would imply under plausible measurement conditions. Because the manuscript does not evaluate the cost or implementation feasibility of particular imaging modalities, we have not added a categorical forecast about routine adoption. Instead, the revised text makes the illustrative status and demanding performance requirements clear by describing the estimated performance as modest and the prospective target as ambitious, in Section 3.2.1:
“Entering these values into E2P Simulator yields ROC-AUC = 0.71 and PR-AUC = 0.66, indicating rather modest predictive performance, as shown by the low PR-AUC (Fig. 5).”
and:
“Using E2P Simulator we find that to achieve PR-AUC = 0.8, it would require explaining approximately 47% of variance (R2 = 0.47), which is rather ambitious.”

disp-quote.p: (6) In the same vein, in section 3.3.2, you write that "predictors are associated with clinical variables". It would help readers if you were more concrete about what types of predictors you are referring to and what differentiates them from clinical variables.

body.p: The earlier wording collapsed three distinct roles: candidate biomarkers, the clinical variables with which they are initially associated, and the outcomes predicted by the combined model. The revised sentence now distinguishes them; in Section 3.2.2:

“When building prediction models in neuroscience, a common approach is to first show that candidate biomarkers are associated with clinical variables (e.g., symptom severity), after which both are jointly used to train a classifier for predicting clinical outcomes (e.g., Hauke et al., 2022; Tozzi et al., 2020; de la Salle et al., 2022; Karvelis et al., 2022).”

disp-quote.p: (1) My main concern with E2P is mainly related to the sample size calculation for multivariable models based on Riley et al. 2020, which goes wrong for machine learning. Riley refers to van der Ploeg et al. 2014, in which they don't consider standard machine learning procedures such as feature selection, tuning, etc. Empirical learning curves show that sample size calculations are way off. But as sample size calculations are not covered in this manuscript, please ignore for now, but I hope the authors can incorporate something more appropriate (synthetic learning curves?).

body.p: Thank you for pointing out these issues. We will look into it and will update this module accordingly. Given that it is beyond the scope of the paper, no changes were made to the manuscript in response to this comment.

disp-quote.p: (2) How do the True vs Observed effects above the figure relate to the True vs Observed effects for the effect size slider in the box on the left? One can only enter values under True, while one only obtains Observed effect sizes. Does this left ES box alternate with the Effects button above? It may be good to provide some additional explanation on when to enter values where.

body.p: The apparent inconsistency arises because the two interface elements operate at different levels. The True/Observed switch above the plot controls which distributions and predictive metrics are displayed; it does not alter the paired True and Observed effect size values shown in the left panel. Those values remain linked through the reliability settings. Because the numeric field edits the latent True value, a user reproducing a reported observed effect should first enter the reliability parameters and then move the slider until the Observed value matches the reported result. Box 1 now presents the inputs in that sequence:
“Specify measurement reliability. Enter reliability estimates for the predictor and outcome, preferably from the same dataset or closely matched studies.”
and:
“Enter the observed result. Use an effect size (e.g., Cohen’s d, OR, Pearson’s r) or predictiveperformance metric (e.g., ROC-AUC, PR-AUC).”
We have now also added an interactive tutorial which explains the E2P Simulator’s interface, which will hopefully make the interface more intuitive.

disp-quote.p: (3) A minor comment for the example under 3.1.1: I don't see how the population prevalence is relevant here, as one would only assess depression in a preselected clinical setting. Similarly, for 3.3.1: how is the response to antidepressants beyond placebo relevant, as one is only observing the response, regardless of whether it is related to the compound or placebo?

body.p: Thank you for bringing this up. The two examples require different base rate logic. In the depression example, use of the general population prevalence is not a claim that the biomarker should be deployed for population-wide screening. It follows from the particular case-control effect, which contrasts patients with depression against healthy controls. The revised text makes this conditionality explicit and explains what would be required to analyze a preselected clinical population; in Section 3.1.1:

“Finally, because the effect size in question summarizes the differences between patients and healthy controls, the relevant target population for this illustrative analysis is the general population. Recent national surveys estimate depression prevalence to be around 9.2% among Americans aged 12 years or older (Goodwin et al., 2022) and 7.7% among Canadians aged 15 years or older (Halladay et al., 2026). We therefore use 8% as a rounded illustrative base rate within this range. Note that a more clinically realistic scenario, such as those explored below, would consider the biomarker in a preselected, higher prevalence group (e.g., help-seeking individuals); however, evaluating the biomarker in this setting would require an effect size estimated using controls drawn from that same target population rather than healthy controls from the general population.”

We thank the reviewer for highlighting the inconsistency in the treatment response prediction example: the relevant base rate is indeed the observed response rate among treated patients, not response beyond placebo. We have corrected the value to 46% and updated Figure 5 and all associated results; in Section 3.2.1:
“A recent meta-analysis of SSRI trials reported a 46% response rate, defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in MADRS scores (Hieronymus et al., 2025); we therefore use 46% as the base rate…

…ROC-AUC = 0.71 and PR-AUC = 0.66, indicating rather modest predictive performance, as shown by the low PR-AUC (Fig. 5). We use an illustrative threshold of pt = 0.20 to examine classification of likely responders among patients receiving antidepressant treatment. At pt = 0.2, we observe sensitivity = 0.98 and PPV = 0.48, meaning that 88% of nonresponders would still be classified as likely responders. This would correspond to ∆NB = 0.005 or 5 additional correctly identified responders per 1,000 patients evaluated. Under these proxy reliability assumptions, perfect measurement would improve performance quite substantially, up to ROCAUC = 0.85 and PR-AUC = 0.83, which at pt = 0.2 would result in sensitivity = 0.95, PPV = 0.59, and ∆NB = 0.035.”

disp-quote.p: My more directed recommendations are to reformulate the examples to consider the potential end users of this tool. As stated in the public review, I think this will significantly improve the clarity around the manuscript.

body.p: We appreciate this recommendation; it became an organizing principle for the revision. The manuscript is now structured around two end user tasks: evaluating the practical significance of an existing finding and planning future research around a clinically meaningful performance target; in Section 2.5, we say:

“Predictive utility analysis can be used both to evaluate existing findings and to plan new studies (Box 1). When evaluating an existing finding, researchers can work forward from a reported effect size or model performance estimate to examine its expected predictive value and utility in the target population. When planning research, they can work backward from a desired level of predictive performance (Lord et al., 2019) to determine which combinations of effect size or discriminative performance, measurement reliability, outcome base rate, and number of predictors would achieve that target. This is analogous to power analysis (Cohen, 1992): whereas power analysis evaluates whether a study is likely to detect an effect under specified assumptions, predictive utility analysis evaluates whether an effect or model is likely to provide meaningful practical utility under specified assumptions.
The newly added Box 1 and Section 4.1 also provide more guidance on how to perform predictive utility analysis beyond the provided examples.
